Difference and system GMM for dynamic linear panel models

Source: R/pangmm.R
pangmm.Rd

Arellano and Bond (1991) difference GMM and Blundell and Bond (1998) system GMM for linear panel models with a lagged dependent variable and an unobserved individual effect, y_it = sum_j rho_j y_i,t-j + x_it'b + mu_i + e_it. Both one-step and two-step estimators are available, with robust one-step and Windmeijer (2005) corrected two-step standard errors, the Arellano-Bond tests for first- and second-order serial correlation of the differenced residuals and the Sargan and Hansen tests of the overidentifying restrictions.

Usage

pangmm(
  formula,
  data,
  index,
  transformation = c("d", "ld"),
  model = c("onestep", "twostep"),
  effect = c("twoways", "individual"),
  collapse = FALSE,
  maxlag = NULL,
  vcov = c("robust", "classical", "cluster")
)

Arguments

formula

a formula y ~ regressors | gmm instruments or y ~ regressors | gmm instruments | standard instruments; see the Formula section

data

a data.frame in long format

index

length-2 character vector giving the individual and time columns

transformation

"d" (difference GMM, Arellano-Bond) or "ld" (system GMM, Blundell-Bond)

model

"onestep" or "twostep"

effect

"twoways" (time dummies, the default) or "individual"

collapse

logical: collapse the GMM-style instruments to one column per lag (and, for system GMM, one column for the level equation). A named logical vector applies it to selected GMM variables, named as in the formula, e.g. c("log(bmi)" = TRUE).

maxlag

optional positive integer: the largest lag of the GMM-style instruments, overriding larger upper lags in the formula (lag(y, 2:99) with maxlag = 4 uses lags 2 to 4)

vcov

"robust" (one-step sandwich or Windmeijer-corrected two-step, both clustered by individual) or "classical"; "cluster" is accepted as a synonym of "robust", the name used by the other estimators of the package. See vcov.pangmm() to switch after fitting

Value

an object of class "pangmm", a list with components coefficients (the final estimates; time dummies are named by their period), coefficients_onestep, vcov, vcov_type, vcov_list (the classical and robust covariances), residuals (one numeric vector per individual, differenced rows first and, for system GMM, level rows after; rows not used are zero), artest (data frame of the Arellano-Bond tests), sargan, hansen and wald (lists with statistic, df and p.value; wald tests the joint significance of the coefficients other than time dummies and the constant), sigma2 (s2), n_instruments, nobs (number of equations used), nobs_diff, nobs_level, n_groups, n_periods, timedummies (names of the time-effect coefficients), transformation, model, effect, collapse, call and formula. Methods: print, summary, coef, vcov, confint, predict, residuals, nobs, tidy and glance.

Formula

The formula follows plm::pgmm() and has two or three parts separated by |:

y ~ lag(y, 1) + x + lag(x, 1) | lag(y, 2:99) | z

  • The first part lists the regressors. lag(v, k) is the lag of order k of v within the individual, k may be a vector (lag(v, 0:2) gives v and its first two lags) and lag(v) means lag(v, 1). Any expression of the data can be lagged, e.g. lag(log(bmi), 1). The intercept is not estimated: the individual effects are differenced out, and time effects or the system-GMM constant are added through effect.

  • The second part lists the GMM-style instruments: lag(v, a:b) uses, for the differenced equation of period t, the levels v_(t-a), ..., v_(t-b) that exist in the panel (b = 99 means all available lags). For an endogenous variable a = 2, for a predetermined one a = 1.

  • The optional third part lists standard (IV-style) instruments, with the same lag() syntax; each enters in first differences in the differenced equation (and in levels in the level equation of system GMM). Without a third part, every regressor whose variable does not appear among the GMM-style instruments is used as its own standard instrument, as in plm::pgmm().

Lags are taken on the time grid formed by the sorted distinct values of the time index, so missing waves are respected and waves need not be equally spaced in calendar time (plm instead lags by the numeric value of the time index, so biennial waves coded as years have no lag one period back there); rows with a missing value in the response or a regressor are dropped from the moment conditions and missing instruments are set to zero, as in plm and Stata's xtabond2.

Estimators

With transformation = "d" (difference GMM) the model is estimated in first differences, with the GMM-style instruments of each period in their own columns (block-diagonal instrument matrix) or, with collapse = TRUE, one column per lag (Roodman 2009). The one-step weight matrix is (sum_i Z_i' H Z_i)^-1 with H the tridiagonal matrix with 2 on the diagonal and -1 off it, the covariance of the differenced errors under homoskedasticity. With transformation = "ld" (system GMM) the level equations of the same periods are stacked under the differenced ones and instrumented by the first difference of each GMM-style variable lagged a - 1 periods (a its smallest lag); the one-step weight uses the block matrix H = [G, D; D', I] of plm::pgmm() (fsm = "full"). The two-step estimator uses the weight (sum_i Z_i' e_i e_i' Z_i)^-1 built from the one-step residuals.

With effect = "twoways" (the default) time dummies are included: in differences for difference GMM, and for system GMM a constant and time dummies in the level equation (which instrument themselves there). With effect = "individual" there are no time effects; system GMM then keeps a constant in the level equation (plm::pgmm() omits it).

Regressors that are not identified, because they are collinear with the time effects (for instance age in a balanced annual panel, whose first difference is constant) or with each other, are dropped with a warning, as in panglm(); they remain standard instruments when listed as such.

Inference

vcov = "robust" gives the one-step sandwich covariance or, for the two-step estimator, the Windmeijer (2005) finite-sample corrected covariance. vcov = "classical" gives, for the one-step estimator, s2 (X'Z S1^-1 Z'X)^-1 with S1 = sum_i Z_i' H Z_i and s2 = sum(de^2) / (2 (n_d - k)) estimated from the n_d differenced one-step residuals de; for the two-step estimator it gives the conventional (downward biased) (X'Z S2^-1 Z'X)^-1 with S2 = sum_i Z_i' e1_i e1_i' Z_i. (The one-step vcov() of plm::pgmm() is (X'Z S1^-1 Z'X)^-1 / N, without the error variance.)

The Arellano-Bond statistic of order m tests for autocorrelation of order m in the differenced residuals; it is standard normal under the null of no autocorrelation. First-order autocorrelation is expected by construction; second-order autocorrelation indicates that y_(t-2) is not a valid instrument. It is computed with the robust covariance of the fit, as in summary(plm::pgmm()). The Sargan statistic (Z'e1)' (sum Z_i' H Z_i)^-1 (Z'e1) / s2 uses the one-step residuals and is valid only under homoskedasticity; the Hansen J statistic (Z'e2)' (sum Z_i' e1_i e1_i' Z_i)^-1 (Z'e2) uses the two-step residuals and is robust. Both are chi-squared with L - k degrees of freedom (L instruments, k coefficients); plm::sargan() returns the Hansen statistic by default and N s2 times the Sargan statistic with weights = "onestep". Many instruments weaken the Hansen test (Roodman 2009); collapsing or limiting the lag depth keeps the instrument count well below the number of individuals.

Finite-sample bias

The estimators are consistent as the number of individuals grows, but in moderate samples they can be badly biased, and matching another package does not protect against it. Two mechanisms matter. Too many instruments overfit the endogenous regressors and pull the estimate toward pooled OLS, while making the Hansen test look too good (Roodman 2009). And when the variance of the individual effect is large relative to the idiosyncratic variance, the level moments of system GMM become weak and the estimate again drifts toward OLS (Bun and Windmeijer 2010). In a simulated BMI panel (true persistence 0.6, effect SD 1.5, error SD 1, 8 waves, 63 instruments) uncollapsed system GMM averaged 0.78 one-step and 0.72 two-step with 400 individuals, 0.65 and 0.61 with 2000 individuals; collapsing the instruments gave 0.62 already with 400. Practical rules: prefer the two-step estimator, use collapse = TRUE and a small maxlag, keep the instrument count well below the number of individuals (pangmm() warns when it is not), treat a Hansen p-value close to 1 as a warning sign rather than as support, and check that the coefficient of the lagged outcome lies between the fixed-effects (downward biased) and pooled OLS (upward biased) estimates (Bond 2002).

Validation

Checked against plm::pgmm() and its vcovHC(), mtest(), sargan() and pwaldtest() methods (difference and system GMM, one and two steps, with the Windmeijer correction), and predict() against the transformed equations stored by plm::pgmm(), on plm::EmplUK and a simulated unbalanced panel, in the package's validation suite on GitHub.

References

Bond, S. (2002). Dynamic panel data models: a guide to micro data methods and practice. Portuguese Economic Journal, 1, 141-162.

Bun, M. J. G. and Windmeijer, F. (2010). The weak instrument problem of the system GMM estimator in dynamic panel data models. The Econometrics Journal, 13, 95-126.

Arellano, M. and Bond, S. (1991). Some tests of specification for panel data: Monte Carlo evidence and an application to employment equations. Review of Economic Studies, 58, 277-297.

Blundell, R. and Bond, S. (1998). Initial conditions and moment restrictions in dynamic panel data models. Journal of Econometrics, 87, 115-143.

Windmeijer, F. (2005). A finite sample correction for the variance of linear efficient two-step GMM estimators. Journal of Econometrics, 126, 25-51.

Roodman, D. (2009). How to do xtabond2: An introduction to difference and system GMM in Stata. Stata Journal, 9, 86-136.

See also

summary.pangmm(), vcov.pangmm() and predict.pangmm() for the fitted model, tidy-methods for tidy() and glance().

Other panel models: panfmm(), panfmmselect(), panglm(), panhurdle(), paniv(), panqr(), panselect(), twopart()

Examples

# Habit persistence in smoking: cigarettes per day depend on last
# wave's consumption (state dependence) and on the price of tobacco,
# with a permanent individual propensity to smoke. The lagged outcome is
# correlated with that propensity, so pooled OLS overstates persistence
# and the within estimator understates it (Nickell bias); GMM is
# consistent. True values: persistence 0.5, price -0.3.
set.seed(1)
N <- 300; TT <- 7
d <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(N), each = TT), wave = rep(seq_len(TT), N))
propensity <- rnorm(N)
d$price <- rnorm(N * TT)
d$cigs <- NA
for (i in seq_len(N)) {
  r <- (i - 1) * TT + seq_len(TT)
  y <- propensity[i] / 0.5 + rnorm(1)
  for (t in seq_len(TT)) {
    y <- 0.5 * y - 0.3 * d$price[r[t]] + propensity[i] + rnorm(1)
    d$cigs[r[t]] <- y
  }
}

# Arellano-Bond difference GMM, two-step with Windmeijer standard errors
ab <- pangmm(cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), data = d,
             index = c("id", "wave"), model = "twostep")
summary(ab)
#> 
#> Call:
#> pangmm(formula = cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), 
#>     data = d, index = c("id", "wave"), model = "twostep")
#> 
#> Estimator: two-way two-step difference GMM (Arellano-Bond) 
#> N = 300  T = 7  equations used = 1500  instruments = 21  vcov: robust (Windmeijer) 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> lag(cigs, 1)  0.55025    0.04883  11.268   <2e-16 ***
#> price        -0.27276    0.03055  -8.927   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Arellano-Bond AR(1) test: z = -10.24, p = < 2.2e-16
#> Arellano-Bond AR(2) test: z = -0.9451, p = 0.3446
#> Sargan test (not robust): chi2(14) = 7.391, p = 0.9186
#> Hansen J test (robust): chi2(14) = 6.259, p = 0.9595
#> Wald test for coefficients: chi2(2) = 194.5, p = < 2.2e-16
#> 

# Blundell-Bond system GMM with collapsed instruments and at most three
# lags of the outcome as instruments
bb <- pangmm(cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), data = d,
             index = c("id", "wave"), transformation = "ld",
             model = "twostep", collapse = TRUE, maxlag = 4)
summary(bb)
#>

#> pangmm(formula = cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99),

#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

#> Arellano-Bond AR(1) test: z = -8.576, p = < 2.2e-16
#> Arellano-Bond AR(2) test: z = -1.041, p = 0.2978
#> Sargan test (not robust): chi2(4) = 5.905, p = 0.2064
#> Hansen J test (robust): chi2(4) = 4.635, p = 0.3269
#> Wald test for coefficients: chi2(2) = 268.8, p = < 2.2e-16
#> 

# Employment equation of Arellano and Bond (1991)
if (requireNamespace("plm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data("EmplUK", package = "plm")
  emp <- pangmm(log(emp) ~ lag(log(emp), 1:2) + lag(log(wage), 0:1) +
                  log(capital) + lag(log(output), 0:1) | lag(log(emp), 2:99),
                data = EmplUK, index = c("firm", "year"), model = "twostep")
  summary(emp)
}
